title: High Blood Pressure in Pregnant Women Is Rising Across the Country
gist: A new CDC report finds hypertension among US women giving birth rose 73 percent between 2016 and 2024, from just over 6 percent to more than 1 in 10 births, with increases in every state and across every age, race, and weight group — a breadth that points to a systemic driver rather than a shift in who is giving birth.

insights.claim: The rate of high blood pressure among US women who gave birth rose 73 percent between 2016 and 2024, with more than 1 in 10 women giving birth in 2024 having some form of hypertension including preeclampsia, up from a little over 6 percent in 2016.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A near-doubling of maternal hypertension in eight years expands the addressable population for blood-pressure monitoring, preeclampsia diagnostics, and high-risk obstetric care.
insights.quote: The rate of high blood pressure among women who gave birth shot up 73 percent between 2016 and 2024, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control.

insights.claim: Maternal hypertension increased in every US state and for women of every age, race, and weight over the 2016 to 2024 period.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Universality across geography and demographics argues the cause is a common environmental, dietary, or measurement-practice shift rather than any single subgroup's behavior.

insights.claim: American Indian and Alaska Native mothers had the highest rates of hypertension in the CDC report, while Asian women had the lowest rates but still saw their risk double over the eight years studied.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
entities: American Indian and Alaska Native mothers
insights.so_what: Even the lowest-risk group doubled, so disparity narratives do not explain the trend — the whole distribution shifted.

insights.claim: Hypertension incidence in childbirth was lowest for mothers younger than 20 and those aged 30 to 34, and highest for mothers aged 40 and older.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The non-monotonic age curve means rising maternal age alone cannot fully account for the trend, though the 40-plus cohort carries the heaviest clinical load.

insights.claim: Maternal high blood pressure rose with body mass index, but it also increased among underweight mothers during the same eight-year period.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Rising rates in underweight women undercut a purely obesity-driven explanation and keep alternative causes — diet composition, stress, diagnostic thresholds — on the table.

insights.claim: Because the CDC report drew on data collected at birth rather than prior medical tests, the true prevalence of maternal hypertension may be higher than documented.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Birth-record-based surveillance systematically undercounts, so the headline 73 percent increase is likely a floor, not a ceiling.
